steps: Install to CAN/CSA-B365 and local code, with local building-official approval. Not in any fireplace or mobile home; never connect to an air distribution duct or system.

Discuss the installation with the local building officials before you start; they have final authority to approve it. Confirm the stove and chimney connector can meet every clearance and that the floor protection is adequate.

The data plate on the back of the stove gives the safety testing information, the certified testing laboratory and the installation requirements.

Do not install in any fireplace. Do not connect to any air distribution duct or system. Do not install in a transportable building / mobile home (p. 12).

Flatten the carton as a work surface. Take the legs and bolts out of the stove, lay it on its back, unscrew it from the pallet and bolt the legs to the base; lift it upright, avoiding excess load on the back legs.
Confirm the fire bricks haven't shifted, the air control works freely, and the baffle (1), baffle insulation (2) and cover (3, identification number 2118) are placed correctly.

Before the first fire, check:

  • Fire bricks firmly in position, not shifted in transit.
  • Air control works freely.
  • Baffle (1) and the insulation (2) over it placed correctly.
  • Cover (3), identification number 2118, placed correctly.

Smoke cover (p. 6)

Place it by the smoke vent at the front of the stove: lead it down through the flue collar before fitting the pipe, or fit it through the access door opening.

Vertical baffle (p. 7)

Lead it through the door, set it in position and place the baffle insulation on it.

A Morsø glove and the ceramic flue connection gasket are standard accessories, usually found in the ashpan or firebox area (p. 7).

Residential masonry with flue liner or listed HT factory-built (UL-103-1985, 2100º F; ULC S-629 in Canada), not less than 6" inside, one flueway per appliance, independently supported; 16 feet above the stove recommended.

6 inches (150mm) connector: 24 MSG black or blue single-wall (24 gauge or heavier, never galvanized) or listed double-wall. Minimum three screws at the stove and every joint; seal it airtight to the chimney outlet.

Single-wall connectors: 24 gauge or heavier steel. Double-wall connectors: tested and listed for solid-fuel burning appliances. Do not use galvanized connector. Secure with a minimum of three screws to the stove and to each adjoining section, and seal every joint so the system is airtight from the heater to the chimney outlet.

Horizontal run: 3 feet (1 metre) recommended max., total length no longer than 8 feet (2.5 metres), slope upward 1/4 inch per foot (20 mm per metre) toward the chimney, no more than two 90 degree turns, 18 inches from the ceiling. Don't pass the connector through an attic, closet or similar concealed space. Wear gloves and protective eyewear when drilling, cutting or joining sections.

Note: p. 8 says a chimney connector is included with the heater, but p. 7 lists only a glove and a ceramic flue connection gasket as standard accessories, the parts list on pp. 24-25 has no connector pipe, and p. 9 tells you which connector to use.
Single-wall connector minimums (USA and Canada): sidewall 26", backwall 7", cornerwall 22" to the unit; 29", 15" and 29" to the connector. At least 4 inches recommended to non-combustible walls.

Non-combustible floor protection beneath the stove, 16" to the front and 6" to the sides (US); 450 mm and 200 mm in Canada. Add a 2 square inch (1250 square mm) fresh air inlet if room air leakage is insufficient.
Keep the first fire small so the stove paint can cure and the main plates settle into position. The paint gives off some fumes; ventilate the room.

panels.title: Poor draft · smoke or sluggish fire
items: Smoke or fumes when lighting or reloading, or a fire that won't respond → poor draft (in a very few cases, too little fresh air into the room)
Smoke spills when the door opens → open it 1-2" first and wait a few seconds for the flue pressure to equalise
Stove suddenly sluggish → soot fall around the flue collar or in the flue/chimney
Back-puffing and sluggishness → overly dry wood that is gray in color
Sluggish or unpredictable → flue section too large, flue gases cool excessively

panels.title: Excessive draft · over-firing
items: Burns hotter and faster than intended even with the primary air set low → excessive chimney draft
Rapid fuel use, can't hold a low burn, roaring fire sounds → excessive draft
Stove or connector pipe glowing, flue over 450° C (750°F) → over-firing
Fix: reduce the air, burn smaller loads, check the chimney against the manual's dimensions, consult a chimney professional (a listed flue damper may be necessary)

panels.title: Dirty glass
items: Logs too large or not split
Combustion temperatures too low, or the stove run too slowly
Glass persistently mists up and the wood spits or sizzles → wood not properly seasoned

panels.title: Fast internal wear
items: Soot and ashes left to accumulate
Ash built up toward the underside of the grate → trapped heat, premature grate failure
Baffle distorted by an overfire → efficiency may be compromised; replace it
Door hard to close or air leaking around it → hardened door gasket; replace it

light.title: Lighting a fire
light.html:
Morsø recommends the top-down method. It's the most environmentally friendly way to light, and it minimizes soot on the glass.

  1. Use two firelighters and about 2-4 lbs of dry kindling sticks. Put the firelighters directly under the top layer of kindling.
  2. Open the air fully: turn the spinner on the door 2 1/2 turns counterclockwise from closed.
  3. Light the fire.
  4. Close the door partway, leaving it open an inch or two so plenty of air gets in. Don't leave the stove while the door is open.
  5. After about 5-10 minutes, once the chimney is warm, close the door. Keep the spinner at least 1-1 1/2 turns open while the kindling burns.

A good layer of embers forms after about 15-20 minutes. Then you can add logs (see Reload the stove).

Your very first fire should be small, so the paint can cure and the main plates can settle. The paint gives off some fumes, so ventilate the room.
Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire. Build the fire directly on the firebox floor; the manual says not to raise it with a grate, andirons or anything similar.

air.title: Air control & draft
air.html:
The spinner on the door controls the primary air. Opening it lets preheated air into the firebox through the airwash above the glass. The secondary air, injected into the gases above the fire for cleaner burning, is fixed open and can't be adjusted.

Fully open2 1/2 turns counterclockwise from closed
Medium burn1-1 1/2 turns counterclockwise
Closedminimum low burn rate

Even closed, a small factory-set gap (1.8 mm) stays open for the minimum burn rate. Don't alter it; that's against federal regulations. Before burning on minimum, let the fire burn at medium for about 15 minutes.

Rule of thumb: less heat, less wood, less air. More heat, more wood, more air. Keep a good layer of embers either way.

Smoke or a roaring fire?

Smoke coming out when you light or reload, or a fire that won't respond, almost certainly means poor draft. Ask your stove supplier about improving the flue. A fire that burns hot and fast even on low air, roars, or makes the stove or pipe glow means too much draft: turn the air down as far as it goes, burn smaller loads and call a qualified chimney professional.

reload.title: Reloading the stove
reload.html:
Add wood while there are still glowing embers in the bed. The new logs should catch within a minute or two.

  1. Use a poker to spread the embers across the firebox floor, with most of them toward the front.
  2. Open the door gently, just 1-2" at first. Wait a few seconds for the pressure in the flue to equalise, then open it all the way. This stops smoke spilling out, especially when the draft is poor.
  3. Load 4 lbs (2 pieces) up to 7 lbs (5 pieces). Keep the wood below the lowest secondary air nozzles and no higher than the top edge of the back stone lining.
  4. Close the door and open the spinner fully, 2 1/2 turns counterclockwise.
  5. After a few minutes, adjust the air to suit the heat you want.
Don't open the door while the fire is burning vigorously. If the new logs don't ignite, in an extreme case the flue gases can ignite, so always reload onto a good layer of embers.
Note: p. 16 recommends a load of 4 lbs (2 pieces) up to 7 lbs (5 pieces) and p. 17 gives a maximum of 3.5 kg/7 lbs per load, but the safety summary on p. 28 says to use 2 - 3 pieces, no more than 2 - 2.5 kg, when refuelling.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn natural wood only, and only when it's well seasoned and dry, with no more than 20% moisture. The Morsø Moisture Meter (part # 62929900) makes that easy to check.

Lengthmax 18 inches (45 cm)
Thicknessapprox. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm)
Weight per piecearound 2-4 lbs

Split logs down the middle so moisture can escape, and stack them under cover where air moves through each piece. Some softwoods are ready after one good summer; oak, maple and elm can take up to 18 months.

Dry enough? Seasoned wood feels light and shows cracks running out from the center at the ends. If the wood spits or sizzles and the door glass keeps misting up, it isn't properly seasoned. Overly dry gray wood can cause back-puffing and a sluggish fire.

Never burn

Garbage, lawn clippings or yard waste, materials containing rubber (including tires), materials containing plastic, waste petroleum products, paints or paint thinners, asphalt products, materials containing asbestos, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties or pressure-treated wood, manure or animal remains, salt-water driftwood or other previously salt-water-saturated materials, unseasoned wood, or paper products, cardboard, plywood and particleboard. Fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

Burning these materials may release toxic fumes, or make the heater ineffective and cause smoke.

Note: p. 13 gives a log thickness of approx. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm) in section; the safety summary on p. 28 says the fuel must be split and 8 - 12 cm thick.

ash.title: Emptying the ash pan
ash.html:
Empty the ash pan daily, or as needed. Ash that builds up toward the underside of the grate traps heat and can make the grate fail early.

  1. Open the front door. Use a shovel or poker to stir the excess ash through the slots in the grate into the ash pan.
  2. Take out the ash pan, keeping it level so ash doesn't spill.
  3. Empty the ash into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid.
  4. Put the ash pan back in place and close the door.

Set the closed container on a noncombustible floor or on the ground, well away from anything that can burn, until final disposal. If you bury or scatter the ashes, keep them in the closed container until all cinders have thoroughly cooled.

If you can, keep a 1-1.5 inch (2-3 cm) layer of ash on the floor of the firebox. It adds insulation.
Never empty the stove while it's in operation. Never use a household or shop vacuum cleaner to remove ash.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
When the stove runs at the right temperature there should be little or no dirt on the glass. Dirt that settles while you light it mostly burns off as the fire gets hotter.

For heavier deposits that won't burn off, use Morsø glass cleaner on cold glass, following its instructions. Never use abrasive cleaners.

Why the glass gets dirty

  • Wood that is too wet or not well seasoned
  • Logs too large or not split
  • A fire burning too cool, or the stove run too slowly

Lighting top-down and building a layer of hot embers keeps soot to a minimum.

Cracked or broken glass: don't use the stove until it's replaced, and use only the high temperature ceramic glass supplied by Morsø (ask your Morsø dealer). To avoid breaking it, don't strike the glass or slam the door.
Old ceramic glass can't go in ordinary glass recycling. Hand it in at a recycling station as ceramic glass.

chimney.title: Chimney & creosote
chimney.html:
A slow fire gives off tar and vapors that condense in a cool chimney as creosote. If creosote ignites it makes an extremely hot fire, so it has to be removed.

  • At least once every two months in the heating season, inspect the chimney and chimney connector for creosote buildup.
  • Every month or so at first, check for soot above the baffle plate and around the flue outlet.
  • If the stove suddenly turns sluggish, check for a soot fall around the flue collar or in the chimney.
  • After each heating season, clean the flue all the way to the top. Before the next season, check that no bird's nests or other blockages have formed.

To look up the chimney, let the stove cool completely and sight up through the flue collar with a mirror. If you can't inspect or clean it yourself, contact your Morsø dealer or a professional chimney sweep.

If you have a chimney fire, act promptly:
1. Close the air control.
2. Get everyone out of the house.
3. Call the Fire Department.

safety.title: Safety & over-firing
safety.html:
• The stove is hot while in operation. Keep children, clothing and furniture away; touching it can burn skin.
  • Keep furniture at least 30 inches away, and the same for drying clothes, newspapers and firewood.
  • Run it with the door fully closed, except when lighting and refuelling. Never leave it unattended with the door open: gas and flame can be drawn out of the stove.
  • Fit a smoke detector in the room with the stove, and at least one on each floor, away from the stove and close to sleeping areas. Some areas also require carbon monoxide detectors.

Don't over-fire it

If any part of the stove or chimney connector glows, you are over-firing. That can cause a house fire or permanently damage the stove, and persistent over-firing may void the warranty. In the stove pipe, normal firing runs about 300° C (550°F); above 450° C (750°F) is over-firing. A Morsø Flue Gas Thermometer (part no. 62901200) helps you check.

The safety summary at the back of the manual also says: never burn overnight.
Don't use chemicals or fluids to start the fire, and don't burn garbage or flammable fluids.

care.title: Yearly care & summer storage
care.html:
Before each heating season

  • Thoroughly clean the chimney and chimney connector. Replace damaged connector sections and weak prefabricated chimney sections; have a mason repair a masonry chimney.
  • Check the gaskets for wear or compression, the glass for cracks, and the door and handle for tightness.

Hinges: lubricate the hinges and closing mechanisms once a year, or as needed, with copper grease or another heat-resistant grease.

Door gasket: it hardens over time. Replace it if the door gets hard to close or air leaks in around it and the fire is harder to control. Your stove supplier has a Morsø rope gasket kit.

Paint: clean it with a vacuum's soft brush attachment or a lint-free cloth. If it turns slightly grey, Morsø touch-up spray paint is available; ventilate well the first time you fire it afterwards.

Over the summer

Clean the stove out thoroughly, because leftover ash soaks up moisture and causes rust. Leave the air control slightly open, and fit a chimney cap to keep rain out without blocking the flue. A desiccant such as kitty litter in the ash pan helps absorb moisture; remove it before the heating season.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
If your stove was supplied by an authorised Morsø dealer, Morsø gives a 10-year manufacturer's warranty against manufacturing defects in the main exterior body parts. The limited warranty runs 10 years from the date of purchase and covers repair or replacement of parts that are defective in material or workmanship.

Not covered

  • Improper installation, or use that doesn't follow the manual and Morsø's firing instructions
  • Damage from overheating or burning the wrong fuel
  • Normal wear and tear such as discolored surfaces, and wear parts: smoke deflector plates, grates, refractory stones/plates, glass and sealing materials
  • The flame-path parts (ashpan, grate, firebricks, fire plates, glass, baffle, flue collar), ceramic rope and paint finish (p. 20)
  • Repairs or modifications Morsø didn't authorize
  • Corrosion from lack of maintenance
  • Problems caused by local conditions, draft, or chimney faults

The warranty is void if the stove isn't installed, operated and maintained as the manual says, if it burns materials it isn't EPA-certified for, or if it's modified without authorization.

To make a claim

Contact Morsø Customer Service (info@morsoe.com or +45 96691900) with proof of purchase, the model and serial number, and a description of the problem, with photos if possible.

specEpa.title: EPA test results & listing
specEpa.html:
Heat output (test range)11 811 to 22 017 Btu/hr
Maker's website: Maximum Heat 31,988 BTU/hr.
Efficiency (HHV, B415.1)75 %
Particulate (EPA Method 28R)1.6 g/h
Carbon monoxide (average)0.94 g/min

Certified to the 2020 U.S. EPA particulate emission standards using crib wood. Certified and listed by PFS TECO (Clackamas, Oregon; Report Number F21-679) to UL 1482-2022 (US) and ULC-S627-2023 (Canada). Listed for burning wood only.

Manufacturer-set minimum low burn rate: with the spinner closed, a 1.8 mm gap remains (p. 16). Altering it is against federal regulations.

specFuel.title: Fuel & load
specFuel.html:
FuelWood only, well-seasoned
Max log length18 inches (45 cm)
Sectionapprox. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm)
Moistureno more than 20%
Load4 lbs (2 pieces) up to 7 lbs (5 pieces)
Max per load3.5 kg/7 lbs (approx 5 split logs)
Kindling, first lighting2-4 lbs

Keep the load below the lowest secondary air nozzles and below the top edge of the backwall stone lining. Morsø Moisture Meter: part # 62929900.

Note: p. 16 recommends a refuel load of 4 lbs (2 pieces) up to 7 lbs (5 pieces) and p. 17 gives max 3.5 kg/7 lbs, but the safety summary on p. 28 says 2 - 3 pieces, no more than 2 - 2.5 kg. For log size, p. 13 gives approx. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm) in section and p. 28 says 8 - 12 cm thick.

specFlue.title: Chimney & flue
specFlue.html:
Connector & chimney IDnot less than 6 inches (or equivalent cross section)
Connector6 inches (150mm)
Chimney, USAUL-103-1985 HT (2100º F) or code-approved masonry with flue liner
Chimney, CanadaULC S-629 HT (650ºC)
Height, recommendedat least 16 feet above the stove (not required)

One flueway per appliance; never connect to a flue serving another appliance. The flue system must be independently secured, not supported by the stove, and the chimney must not be installed directly at the outlet: a chimney connector is required. Don't go significantly larger than 6": an oversized section cools the flue gases and makes the stove sluggish or unpredictable.

Height is measured from the flue collar to the top of the chimney. Roof construction, large trees nearby and high altitude can affect draft and height; consult a local chimney sweep or Morsø dealer.

specRun.title: Connector runs
specRun.html:
Horizontal run3 feet (1 metre) recommended max.
Total connector length8 feet (2.5 metres) max.
Upward slope toward chimney1/4 inch per foot (20 mm per metre)
90 degree turnsno more than two
Horizontal run to ceiling18 inches

24 MSG black or blue single-wall (24 gauge or heavier steel) or a listed double-wall connector tested for solid fuel. Never galvanized. Secure with a minimum of three screws to the stove and to each adjoining section, and seal the joints airtight.

Use mild bends (45º vs. 90º), form one continuous section rather than venting into a large void, and keep every part accessible for cleaning. Avoid combustible walls and ceilings; where a pass-through is unavoidable, follow CAN/CSA-B365, local codes and the chimney manufacturer's instructions. Never through an attic, closet or similar concealed space.

specClear.title: Clearances to combustibles
specClear.html:
Standard residential installation with a single-wall connector. These are the minimum tested distances; increase them for heat-sensitive materials.

A · Sidewall to unit26" (660 mm)
B · Backwall to unit7" (178 mm)
C · Cornerwall to unit22" (559 mm)
D · Sidewall to connector29" (737 mm)
E · Backwall to connector15" (381 mm)
F · Cornerwall to connector29" (737 mm)

The same values apply in the USA and Canada (mm given for Canada). Unit to ceiling and floor to ceiling are shown as "-". The manual lists no double-wall connector clearances.

Non-combustible walls: at least 4 inches (100 mm) recommended for cleaning access and air circulation. Furniture: 30 inches recommended minimum.

specFloor.title: Floor protection
specFloor.html:
Meets CAN/ULC-S627 for a combustible floor without radiant floor protection (p. 11); ember protection is still required.

US · front16"
US · right / left side6"
US · back-
Canada · front450 mm (18 in)
Canada · sides / back200 mm (8 in)

US: non-combustible material beneath the heater, extending 16" to the front and 6" to the sides of the fuel loading door and ash removal openings.

Canada (CSA B365): a continuous, durable, non-combustible ember pad. The 450 mm on a door side runs the full width of the appliance plus 200 mm each side. Installed less than 200 mm from a wall, the pad need only reach the base of the wall. Not on carpet unless structurally supported against displacement and distortion.

specTemp.title: Flue temperature
specTemp.html:
Normal firing, averageapprox. 300° C (550°F)
Maximum450° C (750°F)
Measuredin the stove pipe, 20 cm above the stove

Above 450°C (750°F) counts as over-firing and may cause premature wear. The Morsø Flue Gas Thermometer (part no. 62901200) attaches magnetically to the stove pipe approx 20 cm (8") above the top plate and reads the pipe's surface temperature.

specAir.title: Room air supply
specAir.html:
Fresh air inlet2 square inches (1250 square mm) of free air space
Maker's website: Outside Air Supply Not available. Install to the manual.

Needed unless ambient leakage through doorways, windows and the like is sufficient; particularly important in a well-sealed room or where an extractor hood or ventilation system disturbs the natural air pressure.

Don't place the inlet on a wall usually under negative pressure from the normal wind pattern, or directly across the room from the stove (cold draft).

conflicts.issue: Refuel load: 4 lbs (2 pieces) up to 7 lbs (5 pieces) on p. 16 and max 3.5 kg/7 lbs (approx 5 split logs) on p. 17, vs '2 - 3 pieces of wood - no more than 2 - 2.5 kg' in the p. 28 safety summary. Also flagged in specFuel.
Log thickness: 'approx. 3 to 3.5 inches (7-8 cm) in section' on p. 13 vs 'split and 8 - 12 cm thick' on p. 28. Also flagged in specFuel.

p. 8 says 'A chimney connector is included with the heater', but the standard accessories on p. 7 list only a glove and ceramic flue connection gasket, the parts list (pp. 24-25) has no connector pipe, and p. 9 specifies which connector to use.

catalog_mismatches.manual: heat at rates ranging from 11 811 to 22 017 Btu/hr (EPA test conditions); no other output figure given

no outside-air connection for the stove is described; a dedicated fresh air inlet with 2 square inches (1250 square mm) of free air space is needed unless there is sufficient ambient leakage of air into the room

review.notes: Single 28-page manual (pdftotext); no French-only or scrambled-font text. Catalog efficiency 75 (HHV), emissions 1.6 g/h, log length 18 in, flue 6 in, EPA 2020 crib wood and no mobile-home approval all match the manual. Not checkable: the manual text gives no heating area, firebox volume, height/width/depth, weight or model number (catalog 64209521); catalog features 'tertiary air' and '7 x 21-1/2 in firebox' do not appear (manual names primary airwash air and fixed secondary air only). Clearance (p. 11) and floor-protection (p. 12) values transcribed from the text tables, which label every letter; drawings not used. Only single-wall connector clearances are given; unit-to-ceiling and floor-to-ceiling are '-'. p. 13 says 'do not use a grate, andirons... build fire directly on hearth' while the stove has its own riddling grate with ash slots (p. 21; parts 13-15 on p. 24); the guide repeats the rule (as 'build it on the firebox floor') and describes ash removal through the grate per p. 21. A reviewer may want to clarify. Cross-reference slip: lighting step 2 (p. 15) says 'see box on page 15' for the closed position; that box is on p. 16. p. 16 also prints '1-11/2 turns' for medium burn; read as 1-1 1/2, as printed on p. 15. Smoke detector: p. 16 recommends one in the stove room; p. 18 says detectors go away from the appliance near sleeping areas; both included. Kindling 2-4 lbs (p. 15) vs 1 - 2 kg (p. 28) treated as consistent. 'Never burn overnight' appears only in the p. 28 safety summary; included as stated. No troubleshooting table: fault panels built from Draft conditions (p. 17), Reasons for dirty glass (p. 19), Reasons for fast internal wear (p. 20) and related text. No code table, so codes is empty. Parts diagram (p. 23) not used. p. 10 has no extractable text (QA warning; likely the 'Typical Factory-Built or Masonry Chimney Installations' drawings captioned on p. 8). p. 9 refers to 'the sections on Wall Pass-Throughs', but no such section appears in the text, so the guide gives only the p. 9 rule (CAN/CSA-B365, local codes, chimney maker's instructions).
